The cameras allow people to see and marvel at the natural drama without participating in the unfortunate overcrowding and disturbances to the bears and other wildlife. Research has shown that many sensitive bears must avoid Brooks River.

Life expectancy is an inadequate measure used on its own. Ideally, there would also be a measure of life expectancy that adjusts for any period of extended mobility impairment and/or reduced cognitive function at the end of life (i.e., such that it creates a state of dependence). Admittedly, this would be a very difficult measure to create, however, it would provide more information and context for life expectancy numbers. As an example, Japan has one of the highest life expectancies in the world (I believe 2nd behind Monaco) and they also have a comparatively low rate of degenerative diseases such as Alzheimer Disease. By comparison, life expectancy in Canada is slightly lower than that of Japan, however, rates of degenerative disease are much higher, and an adjusted life expectancy would push Canada down the rankings. It would probably be easier to provide a descriptor alongside life expectancy that indicates rate and prevalence of degenerative disease: high, medium, low.

What strikes me as most significant is that water drawn from the "high-level aquifer" is already brackish and approaching the point of not being drinkable. That most likely indicates that the Ghyben-Herzberg freshwater lens under Lanai is relatively small and thin -- probably an ongoing natural condition (since Lanai sits somewhat in Maui's "rain shadow") and partly due to historic long-term depletion for agriculture. It's an obvious fact of nature that one can't continue drawing more fresh water from this lens than it receives from natural "recharging" processes, without depleting it. Excess withdrawal causes the "mixing zone" of brackish water to rise upward, and eventually freshwater wells start turning brackish. That the high-level aquifer water is brackish is great cause for concern -- and fiddling with the definition of "potable" so it can continue to be used for golf course irrigation is turning a blind eye to the problem and will only make it worse and more intractable.

If the Ethics Commissioner says there are a number of ways to deal with a minister's assets, one of which is a blind trust but another of which is a holding company of sorts, then using the latter is NOT a "loophole". It is simply an alternative method of dealing with potential conflicts. A loophole is a technical exception that allows the person using it to avoid the policy consequence of the main rule. That is not what is happening here. The Ethics Commissioner ruled that it was acceptable, i.e. ethical, for the assets to be held indirectly. So ministers doing so are not crooks or dishonest or unethical. It may be as a matter of optics that a blind trust may be preferable. It may be that the rule should be changed to require a blind trust. But in the meantime, the fact that the rule does not require one does not make the use of any other method of distancing oneself from one' assets a loophole. Calling it that leads to sloppy accusations.
